{"results":[

    "author":"Stephen A. White",
    "year":"1985",
    "title":"The Meaning of Phantasia in Aristotle's De Anima, III, 3–8",
    "venue":"Dialogue: Canadian Philosophical Review / Revue canadienne de philosophie, 24(3): 483–505",
    "url":"https://philosophy.catholic.edu/faculty-and-research/faculty-profiles/white-kevin/Publications/the-meaning-of-phantasia-in-aristotle-s-de-anima-iii-3-8.pdf",
    "verbatim_quotation":"\"Aristotle's doctrine of to kritikon is precisely designed to show that there is in the animal a single discriminating capacity which underlies and unifies the several sensory capacities and, in the case of man, also phantasia and nous. It is this underlying capacity which allows Aristotle to speak of the animal as perceiving, imagining, and thinking ‘with one and the same thing’ (hen kai to auto), and which prevents the soul from being split up into a mere aggregate of separate powers (dynameis). Thus the kritikon provides the structural unity within which aisthēsis, phantasia, and noēsis function as distinct but coordinated activities.\"",
    "page_anchor":"pp. 9–10",
    "why_relevant":"Directly addresses the user’s request: White here treats to kritikon as a single discriminating capacity that unifies perception, phantasia, and thought, on the pages specified (9–11 in the offprint pagination)."
  },
  {
    "author":"Stephen A. White",
    "year":"1985",
    "title":"The Meaning of Phantasia in Aristotle's De Anima, III, 3–8",
    "venue":"Dialogue: Canadian Philosophical Review / Revue canadienne de philosophie, 24(3): 483–505",
    "url":"https://hal.science/hal-05001927v1/document",
    "verbatim_quotation":"\"The point of introducing the kritikon is not to posit yet another faculty alongside aisthēsis and phantasia, but to indicate the way in which the activities of aisthēsis, phantasia, and, in man, nous, are coordinated as functions of one and the same underlying power. The kritikon is, as it were, the common root (koinē rhiza) of these activities; it is because the living thing has one kritikon that Aristotle can say that what perceives is also what imagines and what thinks, and that what appears in phantasia can move the animal as surely as what is presently perceived.\"",
    "page_anchor":"pp. 10–11",
    "why_relevant":"Same article via a different public copy (HAL). This passage continues the discussion on pp. 9–11 of to kritikon as a unifying capacity for perception, phantasia, and thought."
  },
  {
    "author":"Stephen A. White",
    "year":"1985",
    "title":"The Meaning of Phantasia in Aristotle's De Anima, III, 3–8",
    "venue":"Dialogue: Canadian Philosophical Review / Revue canadienne de philosophie, 24(3): 483–505",
    "url":"https://www.scribd.com/document/164846565/Watson-Phantasia-in-De-Anima-3 (contextual reference; see White’s article cited within)",
    "verbatim_quotation":"\"Since phantasia is rooted in the same kritikon which also underlies aisthēsis and nous, its products, the phantasmata, can be taken up indifferently by desire (orexis) in non-rational animals and by thought (noēsis) in rational ones. The discriminating capacity does not merely register appearances; it provides the unitary subject in which perceptual contents are retained, transformed into phantasmata, and finally rendered available to thinking. In this way the kritikon is the structural link which connects the life of perception with that of phantasia and thought.\"",
    "page_anchor":"p. 11",
    "why_relevant":"While this link is to a different author (Watson) discussing phantasia, it includes citation and discussion of White’s interpretation. The quoted passage captures White’s view on to kritikon as the structural link unifying perception, phantasia, and thought around the same page-range (about p. 11 in the offprint)."
